c.tagline: Jamaica's pulsing capital, birthplace of reggae and Blue Mountain coffee.

taxi.fareNote: Use licensed JUTA taxis (red PP plates) and agree the fare before setting off, as most aren't metered. Shared 'route taxis' run fixed routes for a couple of dollars but aren't ideal for visitors with luggage; avoid unmarked cabs, especially at night.

avoid.reason: Avoid inner-city garrison communities — Trench Town, Tivoli Gardens, Denham Town, August Town. Periodic states of emergency.

hood_desc: The uptown business and hotel hub along Knutsford Boulevard, home to most of the city's hotels, banks, embassies, restaurants, and the busiest bars and clubs; the standard and safest base for visitors.
A leafy, upscale residential district north of the centre near the University of the West Indies, quieter and green; suits travellers who want calm and are happy to taxi in and out.
St Andrew's bustling commercial core and transport interchange around the historic clock tower, with shopping plazas, markets, and street food; lively by day and the city's main crossroads.

The historic waterfront and old commercial core, home to the National Gallery of Jamaica, the harbourfront, Coronation Market, and the reggae heritage of nearby Trench Town; rich in sights but best explored by day with a guide or driver.
Upscale hillside residential neighbourhoods on the northern edge of the city, calm and green, and the gateway to the Blue Mountains and their coffee estates; quiet, scenic, and car-dependent.

transit.hours: JUTC city buses run from roughly 5:00 AM to around 10:00-11:00 PM; shared route taxis fill the gaps but thin out and are best avoided after dark.
transit.note: The state-run Jamaica Urban Transit Company (JUTC) operates city buses across the Kingston Metropolitan Region, supplemented by shared 'route taxis' and minibuses on routes buses don't cover. There is no rail or metro. Licensed JUTA taxis and ride apps are the recommended way for visitors to get around, especially at night.
transit.pay: JUTC buses use a rechargeable Smarter Card (or exact cash on some routes); route taxis are paid in cash directly to the driver.

landmarks: Bob Marley Museum
The reggae legend's former home and Tuff Gong-era studio at 56 Hope Road preserves his gold records, guitars and bullet-scarred rooms.
Devon House
The stately 1881 mansion of Jamaica's first black millionaire offers heritage tours, craft shops and the island's most famous I-Scream ice cream.
Port Royal
Once the wickedest city on Earth, this sunken pirate capital across the harbour keeps Fort Charles, Giddy House and buccaneer lore alive.
Blue Mountains
Misty peaks rising behind Kingston produce world-renowned coffee and reward day-trippers with plantation tours, cool air and a sunrise summit hike.
Emancipation Park
Home to the striking Redemption Song statue, this manicured New Kingston park is the city's symbol of freedom and favourite evening jogging spot.
Hope Botanical Gardens and Zoo
The Caribbean's largest public botanical gardens spread 200 acres of royal palms, bougainvillea and lawns beneath the Blue Mountain foothills.
National Gallery of Jamaica
The Caribbean's oldest national art museum showcases Edna Manley, Kapo and Jamaica's intuitive masters in an engaging downtown waterfront setting.
Trench Town Culture Yard
The government yard where Bob Marley learned guitar and wrote No Woman No Cry is now a heritage museum in reggae's birthplace neighbourhood.
Tuff Gong Recording Studio
Founded by Bob Marley in 1965, this working studio still cuts vinyl and offers tours through the beating heart of reggae production.
Lime Cay
A tiny uninhabited islet of white sand and clear shallows, a short boat hop from Port Royal and Kingston's favourite weekend beach escape.

train.note: Jamaica's railway - one of the oldest outside Europe and North America, opened in 1845 - stopped carrying scheduled passengers in 1992, and the Jamaica Railway Corporation now moves only bauxite and occasional freight. Kingston's terminus on Pechon Street stands derelict, and although restoration of a Kingston-Spanish Town-Montego Bay service has been announced several times, nothing is running. A short tourist train, the Appleton Estate rum train in St Elizabeth, is an excursion rather than transport. Jamaica is an island, so there is no international rail.

bus.note: Knutsford Express (https://www.knutsfordexpress.com/) is the comfortable intercity option, running air-conditioned coaches from its terminal on Oxford Road in New Kingston to Ocho Rios, Montego Bay (about 4.5 hours), Negril, Port Antonio, Mandeville and Savanna-la-Mar; book online, as popular departures sell out. Cheaper route taxis and minibuses work out of the Half Way Tree transport centre and the downtown Parade terminus, charging a few hundred dollars and leaving when full, while the state-owned Jamaica Urban Transit Company runs the city buses and the Kingston-Spanish Town-Portmore services. There are no international coach services from Jamaica.

intl.to: Port Royal (Jamaica) - from the downtown Kingston waterfront pier, ~25-30 min across the harbour
intl.op: Port Authority of Jamaica ferry — tickets at the pier

ferry.note: The only scheduled boat is the small government ferry across Kingston Harbour to Port Royal, a 25-30 minute ride from the downtown waterfront near Ocean Boulevard; it has run intermittently while the historic town is redeveloped, so check that it is operating before relying on it. Port Royal also has a floating cruise pier, but that takes cruise calls rather than scheduled services. There are no international ferries to or from Jamaica - no boat links to Cuba, Haiti or the Cayman Islands, and cargo ships do not carry passengers - so onward island-hopping means flying.
